h.strategy: Before proposing, briefly model the system: which components carry most of the signal, which are redundant, and where saturation, bottlenecks or substitution between components could occur. Then propose hypotheses that each test a DIFFERENT mechanism (e.g., redundancy, saturation/diminishing returns, bottleneck, interference, compensation, sign reversal). Prefer interactions where the intuitive answer is plausibly wrong, including cases where a usually helpful edit should help LESS or even hurt. Use varied edit fields, condition fields and both directions; no two hypotheses may share the same edit-condition pair or the same underlying reason. Each 'why' must name a concrete mechanism and what pattern would falsify it, not just say a component 'matters more'.

hyps.why: With edge 1 removed the cell is weaker and has more headroom, so a conv on the exit edge gains more.
A strong conv on the direct edge saturates accuracy, so an added conv on edge 0 gains less.
A parallel conv into the output is partly redundant when edge 4 already supplies strong conv features.
With no direct edge, an extra conv path compensates for the lost route.
Replacing a conv on edge 0 with a skip loses learned features, unlike replacing a weaker op.
Replacing the identity shortcut with a pool removes the best gradient path and blurs the signal.
With a strong conv already on the 0-1-2 route, another conv on 1-3 shows diminishing returns.
Replacing a conv with a pool discards capacity, which is worse than pooling over a weaker op.
Removing a 3x3 conv costs more than removing a pool, skip or none.
Replacing a 3x3 conv on the exit edge with pooling discards learned capacity.
